evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-based tumour infiltrating lymphocyte quantification in patients with triple-negative breast cancer: an independent validation study
evidence.outcome: Independent, masked external evaluation of AI models by assessors independent of developers
evidence.effect: Independent masked deployment of locked models found modest correlation with pathologist sTILs (r 0.375-0.473) and significant prognostic association in unadjusted-for-sTIL models.
evidence.quote: We independently evaluated two previously validated AI pipelines that generate five computationally assessed tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (cTIL) scores by masked, independent deployment of locked models.

evidence.title: Evaluating medical AI under missing information: same-provider judges and human raters change apparent safety
evidence.outcome: Same-provider LLM judge leniency effect on apparent model safety ranking
evidence.effect: Positive same-provider association remained after leniency adjustment (exact permutation p = 0.04; GPT-5.5 ~ +0.10 probability); excluding own-provider judge changed which model over-commits least; Fleiss' kappa 0.65.
evidence.quote: First, judge choice materially changes apparent safety: inter-judge agreement is only moderate (Fleiss' kappa = 0.65), and after adjusting for each judge's general leniency (vote-level logistic regression), a positive same-provider association remains (exact permutation p = 0.04; GPT-5.5 ~ +0.10 on the probability scale) - large enough to change which model appears to over-commit least once its own-provider judge is excluded.
evidence.sample_unit: HealthBench conversations (50-item subsample for clinician rating)

evidence.title: Evaluation of LLMs for Automated Dental-to-Medical Consult Letter Generation: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Agreement between GPT-5 automated self-evaluation and blinded human clinician ratings
evidence.effect: GPT-5's self-evaluation results deviated from human judgment, suggesting potential model-based bias in self-assessment.
evidence.quote: Notably, GPT-5's self-evaluation results deviated from human judgment, exhibiting potential model-based bias.

evidence.title: Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Self-preference bias of LLM judges when scoring HealthBench medical chat rubrics
evidence.effect: SPB skews model scores by up to 10 points on HealthBench; judges can be over 50% more likely to wrongly mark failed rubrics as satisfied for their own outputs on IFEval and LiveCodeBench.
evidence.quote: On HealthBench, a medical chat benchmark with subjective rubrics, we observe that SPB skews model scores by up to 10 points, a potentially decisive margin when ranking frontier models.

evidence.title: Clinician-Level Agreement Without Clinical Caution: LLM Evaluator Limits in Medical AI Benchmarking
evidence.outcome: Lineage-dependent self-preference bias in LLM evaluators scoring outputs of related models
evidence.effect: LLM evaluators preferentially scored architectural siblings, systematic lineage-dependent bias independent of language; evaluator independence requires explicit verification.
evidence.quote: We additionally quantified systematic lineage-dependent biases, where models preferentially scored architectural siblings, an effect independent of language.

evidence.title: The Judge is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation

evidence.effect: Pooled Answer Rank Bias was +1.22 positions in Real-POCQi, and all eight judges favored their own answers; +0.53 to +0.62 positions in MedSP1000.

commentary.bottom_line: One benchmark study found that a same-provider AI judge rated its provider's model more leniently than independent judges did, and three hazard studies show AI judges favoring their own or related models' outputs. No study compared independent with developer-led audits of a deployed clinical tool, so certainty that the practice improves safety is very low.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice. A pathology replay with 1,356 patients evaluated locked models independently but did not compare that evaluation with developer-led assessment. An automated benchmark compared independent and same-provider judges and did not report its setting. Both are offline and neither measured patient outcomes, so serious indirectness and imprecision place certainty at very low.

Self-preference bias skewed HealthBench scores by up to 10 points, and all eight judges in another study favored their own answers. GPT-5's self-evaluation deviated from blinded clinician ratings. In one test of the practice, excluding the own-provider judge changed which model over-commits least. This suggests self-assessment may misrank model safety.

In the pathology test, masked assessors independent of the developers evaluated locked models and found modest correlation with pathologist sTILs (r 0.375-0.473). The study shows that independent evaluation of locked models is feasible offline. It did not report the staffing, time, or workflow burden that such evaluation required.

The CHAI guide and a regulatory discussion paper call for independent evaluators, and the paper extends independence to third-party model developers. A lineage study found that evaluators favored outputs of architectural siblings. This suggests independence criteria may need to address shared model lineage as well as organizational separation.

One hazard study scored 3,800 clinical items that included non-English content and found lineage bias independent of language. Neither test of the practice reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether independent audits detect performance gaps in these groups therefore remains unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study has prospectively compared independent and developer-led evaluations of a clinical AI tool in deployment and measured the number of errors or subgroup performance gaps each approach detects, the effect on patient outcomes, or the cost and staffing each approach requires.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study that tested the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study included non-English benchmark items, but it documented bias and did not test independent assessment. Health systems serving these populations cannot yet rely on evidence that independent audits will surface problems specific to their patients.
